title: If Productive Struggle Is the Goal, You're Doing it Wrong
author: Patrick Dempsey
summary: Patrick Dempsey draws on aviation behavioral engineering research to argue that 'productive struggle' in education is frequently implemented in a way that produces unproductive frustration instead, because designers fail to make the discomfort psychologically intelligible to learners. Aviation safety researchers identified eight behavioral techniques — including occupied time, reciprocity, instrument orientation, executive function engagement, external cues, narration, and exit mode — that make difficult and tedious tasks cognitively manageable. Dempsey argues these same techniques, applied to course design, transform arbitrary difficulty into genuinely productive challenge. The core claim is that struggle becomes productive only when learners understand why they are struggling, can see their progress, and have a clear sense of where the challenge ends. Without that scaffolding, difficulty is just difficulty.
points: Aviation behavioral engineering identified eight specific techniques for making difficult tasks cognitively manageable — and every one of them applies directly to educational design for productive struggle.

The difference between productive struggle and unproductive frustration is not the difficulty level; it is whether the learner understands the purpose of the discomfort and can see the path through it.
'Occupied time' — giving learners something meaningful to do while waiting for a result — reduces the subjective experience of difficulty without reducing the objective demand.

Narration, in which the system or instructor describes what is happening and why, converts opaque difficulty into comprehensible challenge — and comprehensible challenge is what productive struggle actually requires.
'Exit mode' matters: learners tolerate difficulty better when they have a clear sense of when and how it will end. Struggle without a visible endpoint feels like failure, not growth.
quotes: Productive struggle is not a feature of difficulty. It is a feature of how difficulty is designed. The same objective challenge can be productive or demoralising depending entirely on the scaffolding around it.
Aviation engineers did not make cockpits easier. They made difficulty intelligible. That is exactly what educational designers need to do.
If a learner cannot answer the question 'why is this hard right now?' they are probably not productively struggling. They are just confused.
The exit mode finding is the one I find most practically useful: people tolerate difficult things much better when they can see the end. Not the answer — just the shape of when this will be over.
